text: The plan that came out of all this was enormous.
The Hyde Park and Kenwood renewal plan covered eight hundred fifty-six acres, most of the neighborhood.
It marked six hundred thirty-eight buildings to come down.
Planners judged them too crowded, too old, or too far gone to keep.
A lot of them were the older, cut-up apartment buildings along streets like 55th and Lake Park, the cheaper rooms where the newest arrivals, many of them Black, had found a foothold.
The numbers behind that are stark.
Between 1950, when Black families were moving in fast, and 1956, the Black population of the area grew by roughly five hundred percent.
The plan met that arrival by clearing the buildings that had absorbed it.
The taverns and rooming houses of 55th Street, the jazz clubs, the gambling spots, the crowded kitchenette flats, all of it was on the map to be erased.
They were cheap, dense, and alive, and in the language of the plan they were blight.
The clearing started before the big plan was even law.
A separate, earlier project called Hyde Park A and B got approved in 1955, and the first demolition came that May, in 1955, three years before the City Council signed off on the full plan.
Bulldozers were already working while the hearings were still going.
The City Council made the whole thing official on November seventh, 1958.
Kimpton had testified in its favor.
